description: Incremental upgrade path to modernize the repo. Each phase is designed to be mergeable independently to limit blast radius. Phases should be done in order — later phases depend on earlier ones.

phases.name: Rails 5.2 → 6.1
phases.rationale: Rails 6.1 is the last major version that still supports Ruby 2.7, making it the safest first step. Skipping 6.0 is intentional — 6.1 has better LTS-era gem support and a more complete upgrade guide.
known_risks: Zeitwerk autoloader replaces classic autoloader — requires all files to follow naming conventions exactly
Action Mailer, ActiveRecord, and ActiveStorage APIs have deprecation removals between 5.2 and 6.1
sprockets 4 changes manifest.js format — assets:precompile behavior changes

phases.name: Ruby 2.7.7 → 3.1.x + replace therubyracer
phases.rationale: Ruby 3.0 made keyword argument separation mandatory (no longer a warning). Ruby 3.1 is the minimum for the subsequent Rails upgrade. This phase also drops therubyracer, which does not build reliably on Ruby 3.x, replacing it with mini_racer.
known_risks: therubyracer removal can break asset compilation if mini_racer is not added — test assets:precompile explicitly
Ruby 3.0 keyword argument changes (hash-as-kwargs) can cause ArgumentError in app and gem code — run full test suite and watch for failures
coffee-rails still works but CoffeeScript is end-of-life; no urgent action required yet

phases.name: Linux Bullseye → Bookworm (OpenSSL 1.1.1 → 3.0)
phases.rationale: Debian Bookworm (12) ships with OpenSSL 3.0, which is actively maintained. OpenSSL 1.1.1 reached end-of-life in September 2023. Separating the OS bump from Ruby/Rails upgrades makes it easy to bisect if anything breaks.
known_risks: OpenSSL 3.0 deprecates legacy cryptographic algorithms — if any OAuth or JWT configuration uses weak algorithms (MD5, RC4, etc.) it will fail
System library package names occasionally differ between Bullseye and Bookworm — verify apt-get install lines in all Dockerfiles still resolve

phases.name: omniauth 1 → 2
phases.rationale: omniauth 2.x drops GET-based OAuth authorize requests (CSRF fix) and, with Rails/Devise, requires the omniauth-rails_csrf_protection adapter. Shipping it separately from the Rails bump keeps an OAuth regression attributable to this change alone — it is the highest-risk piece of the path, so it ships and gets verified on staging by itself.
known_risks: omniauth 2.x rejects GET /auth/:provider — the sign-in links must become POST buttons (button_to) carrying the Rails authenticity token
The smoke suite can only cover the authorize redirect, not the provider callback — verify Google and GitHub sign-in manually on staging before promoting

phases.name: Rails 6.1 → 7.0
phases.rationale: Rails 7.0 introduces Hotwire as the default and removes several long-deprecated APIs. With omniauth already on 2.x, this phase is a pure framework bump. load_defaults stays at 6.1 here; bumping it to 7.0 is a follow-up so the framework upgrade and the default-behavior changes are separately attributable.

changes.spring: remove spring and spring-watcher-listen (spring 2 is pinned < 3.0 and does not load under Rails 7)
changes.load_defaults: keep 6.1; bump to 7.0 in a follow-up
changes.sass_rails: consider migration to dartsass-rails (sassc-based sass-rails is unmaintained)

known_risks: Rails 7.0 removes several ActiveRecord and ActionView helpers removed in the 6.x deprecation cycle
sass-rails 5.x is effectively unmaintained; dartsass-rails is a drop-in replacement but uses a different sass binary

phases.name: Rails 7.0 → 7.1
phases.rationale: Rails 7.1 adds native async queries, better error pages, and Trilogy adapter support, and is a required stop on the way to 7.2. Ruby stays at 3.1 so the framework bump is isolated.
known_risks: Rails.application.secrets is deprecated in 7.1 (used in app/services/jwt_token_service.rb and config/secrets.yml) — migrate to Rails.application.secret_key_base
Rails 7.1 changes the default serialization format for encrypted attributes — if any model uses encrypts, existing ciphertext may be unreadable without a migration

phases.name: Rails 7.1 → 7.2
phases.rationale: Rails 7.0 and 7.1 are past security support; 7.2 is the first supported target reachable without a Ruby bump (its minimum Ruby is 3.1).
known_risks: Rails.application.secrets is removed in 7.2 — the migration to Rails.application.secret_key_base from phase 6 must be complete
Review all gem dependencies for Rails 7.2 compatibility before upgrading

phases.name: Ruby 3.1 → 3.3/3.4 + puma 5 → 6
phases.rationale: Ruby 3.1 is EOL. Done separately from the Rails bumps so regressions are attributable to the runtime change alone.
known_risks: Newer Rubies remove long-deprecated features (e.g. rb_cData C API) that may affect native gems like pg — verify gem compatibility before upgrading
Ruby 3.4 changes frozen string literal warnings and Hash#inspect output — watch for spec failures that compare inspected output

phases.name: Rails 7.2 → 8.x (long-term target)
phases.rationale: Rails 8.0 ships Solid Cache, Solid Queue, and Solid Cable as first-class options and drops several legacy defaults. This phase is exploratory — evaluate based on ecosystem readiness at the time.
known_risks: Rails 8.0 removes Sprockets as the default asset pipeline in favor of Propshaft — CoffeeScript migration to plain JS would become necessary at this point
Review all gem dependencies for Rails 8 compatibility before upgrading; the ecosystem lagged on 7.0 and 7.1 upgrades historically

standing_notes: CoffeeScript (coffee-rails 4.2.2) is EOL. A migration to plain JavaScript can be done independently of any Rails or Ruby upgrade, and would reduce future risk significantly.
Bootstrap 4.3.1 → 5.x is a separate, design-breaking migration (grid and utility class renames) and is not included in this path. It should be scoped as a standalone UI project.
rubocop 0.57.1 is very old (2018). Each phase should include a rubocop version bump as a secondary task since new cops will flag newly introduced code.
PostgreSQL 16 is already current. PostgreSQL 17 can be adopted opportunistically when the Alpine image becomes stable, with no major compatibility concerns expected.
